Muscle Building

Body recomposition: how to lose fat and build muscle at once

The old rule said you had to bulk to build muscle and cut to lose fat. For many people, that is not true. With the right setup you can do both at once, as long as you know who recomposition suits and how slowly it shows on the scale.

By Khushi Gupta · Reviewed October 2026 · 4 min read

What recomposition is

Body recomposition, or recomp, is gaining muscle and losing fat over the same period. Because the two changes partly cancel out on the scale, your weight may barely move while your waist shrinks, your clothes fit differently and your lifts go up.

It works because your body does not run a single energy budget for every tissue. With enough protein and a strong training signal, muscle can be built from incoming nutrients while stored fat covers part of the energy gap. A 2020 review by Barakat and colleagues in Strength and Conditioning Journal concluded that recomposition is well supported in the research, including in trained lifters.

The catch is speed. Because your body is splitting its resources between two goals, each happens more slowly than it would in a dedicated phase. That makes recomp a great default for people who want steady, sustainable progress without the extremes of bulking and cutting, and a weaker choice for someone with a deadline.

Who it works best for

ProfileHow well recomp works
Complete beginnersVery well
Returning after a long breakVery well (muscle memory)
Moderate to higher body fatWell
Intermediate lifters with sloppy training or dietWell, once those are fixed
Lean, advanced liftersSlowly; dedicated bulks and cuts are usually faster

If you are a beginner who is neither very lean nor carrying a lot of fat, the "skinny-fat" position many people start from, recomp is often the best first move. Our bulking vs cutting guide helps if you are unsure which camp you are in.

Set calories: maintenance or a small deficit

Find your maintenance with the TDEE calculator. Then choose:

  • Maintenance if you are fairly lean and want to prioritise muscle.
  • A small deficit, 10-20% below maintenance, if you have more fat to lose. This is the most common recomp setup.

Avoid big deficits. A deficit above about 25% makes it hard to build muscle, and you are back to a plain cut.

Set protein high

Protein is the engine of recomposition. Aim for 1.8-2.2 g per kg of bodyweight, or about 2.0-2.4 g per kg of lean body mass if you carry more fat. Spread it across three to five meals.

Use the protein calculator for your target, and see the protein guide for food ideas.

Train for muscle, with progression

Recomposition only happens if your training gives your body a reason to build muscle. That means lifting weights three to five times a week, with most sets taken close to failure and a clear plan to add reps or weight over time.

  • Train each muscle group at least twice a week.
  • Aim for roughly 10-20 hard sets per muscle per week.
  • Base sessions on compound lifts such as the squat, Romanian deadlift, bench press and pull-up.
  • Keep cardio moderate. Walking is ideal; it adds to the deficit without eating into recovery.

Good starting programmes include the upper/lower split and the beginner full-body workout.

A sample recomp day

For a 70 kg lifter at maintenance of 2,300 kcal, a 15% deficit gives a target of about 1,950 kcal, with 140-150 g of protein.

MealExampleProteinCalories
BreakfastOvernight oats with whey, berries35 g420
LunchChicken or tofu rice bowl with vegetables40 g550
Pre-workoutGreek yogurt and a banana20 g250
DinnerFish or lentil curry, roti, salad40 g600
EveningGlass of milk10 g130
Totalabout 145 gabout 1,950

On training days, place more of your carbohydrates around your session. On rest days you can keep the same totals; the weekly average is what counts.

Common recomp mistakes

  • Eating too little. A big deficit turns a recomp into a cut, and muscle gain stops.
  • Not training hard enough. Comfortable sets with five reps left in the tank do not give muscle a reason to grow.
  • Judging by the scale. A flat scale is expected. Use the waist, photos and strength.
  • Impatience. Recomposition is slow. Most people who quit after four weeks were making progress they could not yet see.

Sleep is part of the plan

Recomposition is a fine balance, and poor sleep tips it the wrong way. In a 2010 study by Nedeltcheva and colleagues in the Annals of Internal Medicine, dieters who slept 5.5 hours instead of 8.5 lost a much smaller share of their weight as fat and more as lean mass. Seven to nine hours is part of the programme, not an extra.

How to track a recomp

Because the scale can stay flat, you need better measures.

MeasureHow oftenWhat you want to see
Bodyweight (weekly average)Daily weigh-inFlat or slowly falling
WaistWeeklySlowly falling
Main liftsEvery sessionRising
PhotosEvery 4 weeksVisible change in shape
Body fat %MonthlyFalling

The body fat calculator and FFMI calculator are useful monthly checks: if body fat falls while FFMI rises, you are recomposing.

If the scale is flat, your waist is unchanged and your lifts have stalled for a month, you are not recomposing, you are maintaining. Drop calories by 10% or tighten your training.

How long does it take?

Recomposition is slower than a dedicated cut for fat loss and slower than a bulk for muscle gain, but it makes steady progress on both. Beginners often see clear changes in 8-12 weeks. Give it at least three months before judging, and expect it to slow as you get leaner and more experienced. At that point, switching to dedicated bulk and cut phases usually makes sense.

A rough guide for a beginner over 12 weeks: a waist reduction of 3-6 cm, a body fat drop of 2-4 percentage points, clear strength gains on the main lifts, and a bodyweight change of anywhere from a few kilograms down to roughly flat. People returning after a break often see faster changes thanks to muscle memory. Individual results vary widely, so compare yourself only with your own starting point.

Frequently asked questions

Can you build muscle in a calorie deficit?

Yes, especially if you are a beginner, returning after a break or carrying higher body fat. High protein, hard training and a moderate deficit make it possible.

Why is my weight not changing during a recomp?

Because fat loss and muscle gain can roughly cancel out on the scale. Track your waist, photos and strength instead; if those are improving, the recomp is working.

How much protein do I need for body recomposition?

About 1.8-2.2 g per kg of bodyweight per day, spread across three to five meals. If you have a lot of body fat, base it on goal weight or lean mass.

Is recomp good for women?

Yes. The principles are the same for everyone: enough protein, a small deficit or maintenance calories, and progressive strength training.
